etymology: From temple + worship; the ordered worship of God at the sanctuary, by sacrifice, song, and prayer.
biblical_def: Temple worship was the ordered worship of the LORD at His sanctuary—first the tabernacle, then the temple Solomon built—according to all that God commanded by Moses and David. It centred on the appointed sacrifices, offered morning and evening and at the set feasts by the priests of the line of Aaron; on the ministry of the Levites in song and music and service; on the incense, the showbread, the lamps, and the holy place; and on the prayers of the people, for the LORD called His house a house of prayer for all nations. The whole pattern was given by revelation, not invented by men: Moses was charged to make all things according to the pattern shewed him in the mount, and David delivered to Solomon the pattern of all by the Spirit. The temple worship pointed beyond itself to Christ—its sacrifices to His one offering, its priesthood to His eternal priesthood, its holy place to the true tabernacle which the Lord pitched, and not man. With His coming the shadow gave way to the substance, and the hour came when true worshippers worship the Father in spirit and in truth, no longer bound to the mountain or the temple, for God is a Spirit. The dictionary honors the temple worship as the divinely-patterned, sacrifice-centred, Christ-foreshadowing worship of the old covenant, fulfilled and superseded in Christ, and teaching the abiding truth that the worship of God is governed by His command and centred on the atonement He provides.
webster_summary: The divinely-patterned worship of God at the sanctuary by sacrifice, song, and prayer; foreshadowing Christ, fulfilled in Him, and teaching worship by God’s command.

corruption_summary: Temple worship is romanticized as a model for elaborate ceremony, or dismissed as primitive ritual; Scripture shows divinely-patterned, Christ-foreshadowing worship now fulfilled.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors attend the temple worship. The first romanticizes it as a warrant for elaborate ceremony and sensual ritual in Christian worship, as though the shadows were to be carried over into the age of the substance. But the temple worship pointed to Christ, and with His coming the shadow gives way: He is the true sacrifice, priest, and temple, and to revive the old ceremonies is to return to the shadow that has passed. The second error dismisses the temple worship as mere primitive ritual, missing its divine pattern and its testimony to the atonement.

The principle to recover is that the worship of God is governed by His command and centred on the atonement. Nothing in the temple was of man’s devising: Moses made all things according to the pattern shewed him in the mount (Exo 25:40; Heb 8:5)—the seed of the regulative principle. And its centre was sacrifice, the blood that pointed to the cross. Now that Christ has come, true worshippers worship the Father in spirit and in truth (John 4:23), no longer bound to the temple, for the Father seeketh such to worship Him. The temple worship abides as a teacher: worship God His own way, and rest upon the sacrifice He has provided in His Son.

etymology: From rebuild + temple; the restoration of the temple after the Babylonian exile, under Zerubbabel and Joshua.
biblical_def: The rebuilding of the temple is the restoration of the house of the LORD at Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, when Cyrus king of Persia, stirred up by the LORD, proclaimed that the people might return and build. Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest led the returning remnant, set up the altar, and laid the foundation, at which the old men who had seen the first house wept aloud while the young men shouted for joy. The work was hindered by the adversaries of Judah and ceased for years, until the LORD raised up the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, who stirred the people to build, rebuking their care for their own panelled houses while the house of God lay waste. By the word of the LORD the work went forward and was finished, and the house was dedicated with joy. Though this second temple lacked the glory of Solomon’s—the ark, the visible glory—the LORD promised by Haggai that the glory of this latter house should be greater than the former, and that He would fill it with glory—a word fulfilled when the Lord Christ Himself, the Desire of all nations, entered its courts. The dictionary honors the rebuilding of the temple as a testimony to the faithfulness of God to His covenant and His word, to the duty of putting His house and worship before our own ease, and to the surpassing glory that came not in gold but in the presence of the incarnate Son.
webster_summary: The restoration of the temple after the exile under Zerubbabel and Joshua; hindered, then finished by the word of the LORD through Haggai and Zechariah.

corruption_summary: The rebuilding is read as mere national restoration; Scripture frames it as covenant faithfulness, the duty of God’s house before our ease, and the promise fulfilled in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the merely political reading that treats the rebuilding as a national restoration project under Persian patronage, missing its covenantal and prophetic weight. Scripture sees the hand of God throughout: the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus to proclaim the return (Ezr 1:3), and the work prospered through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah and was finished according to the commandment of the God of Israel (Ezr 6:14). The empire was the instrument; the LORD was the builder.

The principle to recover is threefold. First, the faithfulness of God to His covenant and His word: He brought His people back and restored His worship as He had promised. Second, the duty of putting God’s house before our own ease—Haggai rebuked the people for dwelling in their panelled houses while the house of God lay waste (Hag 1:4), and the rebuke still searches a church that lavishes care on its own comfort while the worship of God languishes. Third, the surpassing glory that came not in gold: the LORD promised the latter house a greater glory (Hag 2:9), fulfilled not in splendour of building but in the entrance of the incarnate Son, the Desire of all nations, into its courts.

etymology: From priestly + garments; the holy vestments of the Aaronic priesthood, made for glory and for beauty.
biblical_def: The priestly garments were the holy vestments which the LORD commanded for Aaron and his sons, made for glory and for beauty, that they might minister in the priest’s office. The high priest wore the ephod of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen; the breastplate of judgment set with twelve precious stones bearing the names of the twelve tribes, that Aaron might bear their names upon his heart before the LORD continually; the robe of the ephod with bells and pomegranates; the mitre with a plate of pure gold engraved Holiness to the LORD; the broidered coat, the girdle, and the linen breeches. Every part was significant: the names of the tribes borne on the shoulders and the heart spoke of the priest representing the people before God; the bells that his sound be heard when he went in; the golden plate that he bear the iniquity of the holy things. All the garments were given by revelation and made by men filled with the Spirit of wisdom. They foreshadowed the great High Priest, the Lord Jesus, who bears His people’s names upon His heart, who is clothed in the true holiness the plate proclaimed, and who needs no garments to cover sin, having none. The dictionary honors the priestly garments as a divinely-appointed picture of the mediatorial office, fulfilled in Christ, who represents His people before the Father, bears their names upon His heart, and is Himself the Holiness to the LORD that the golden plate foreshadowed.
webster_summary: The holy vestments of the Aaronic priesthood, made for glory and beauty; figures of the priest bearing the people before God, fulfilled in Christ the great High Priest.

corruption_summary: The garments are claimed to justify ornate clerical vestments, or dismissed as mere ancient costume; they foreshadow Christ’s mediatorial office, now fulfilled.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors attend the priestly garments. The first appeals to them to justify ornate sacerdotal vestments and a sacrificing priesthood in the Christian church—as though the shadow were to be perpetuated. But the Aaronic garments belonged to a priesthood that has passed: Christ is the one High Priest, and the New Testament knows no order of vestmented sacrificing priests, but a priesthood of all believers. The second error dismisses the garments as mere ancient costume, missing their rich significance.

The principle to recover is that the priestly garments foreshadowed the mediatorial office of Christ. Made for glory and for beauty (Exo 28:2), every part preached the gospel: Aaron bore the names of the tribes upon his heart for a memorial before the LORD continually (Exo 28:29), as Christ bears His people upon His heart in heaven; the golden plate, Holiness to the LORD (Exo 28:36), proclaimed the holiness in which the priest must come, which Christ alone possesses perfectly. We have a great High Priest passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God (Heb 4:14); the garments are fulfilled in Him, and the believer needs no earthly priest, having the true and abiding one.

etymology: From priestly + course; the twenty-four divisions of the priests for their orderly service, ordained by David.
biblical_def: The priestly courses were the twenty-four divisions into which David, by the Spirit, ordered the descendants of Aaron for their service in the house of the LORD, that the ministry of the sanctuary might go on continually and in order. The sons of Aaron through Eleazar and Ithamar were divided by lot into four and twenty courses, each headed by a chief man, that they might come in their appointed weeks to minister, the priests of each course serving in turn through the year. So the worship of God was carried on without confusion, every man knowing his charge and his season. This order endured to the days of the New Testament: Zacharias the father of John the Baptist was a priest of the course of Abia, and it was while he executed the priest’s office in the order of his course, his lot being to burn incense in the temple, that the angel Gabriel appeared to him. The priestly courses teach that the worship of God is to be conducted decently and in order, that He is not the author of confusion but of peace in all the churches of the saints, and that even the lot, cast for the courses, is disposed by the LORD. The dictionary honors the priestly courses as a pattern of orderly, continual, divinely-arranged ministry, a witness that the God of order ordains both the substance and the arrangement of His worship, and that faithful service in one’s appointed place is the will of God for His servants.
webster_summary: The twenty-four divisions of the priests, ordained by David for orderly, continual service; a pattern that God’s worship is conducted decently and in order.
webster_full: PRIESTLY COURSES, the twenty-four divisions of the priests for service.

Each served in its appointed week through the year.

A pattern of orderly, continual, divinely-arranged ministry.
scriptures: Now these are the divisions of the sons of Aaron. The sons of Aaron; Nadab, and Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.

corruption_summary: The courses are seen as dry administrative detail; Scripture makes them a pattern of orderly, continual worship, for God is not the author of confusion but of order.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the modern impatience that skips the priestly courses as dry administrative detail, mere lists of names and divisions unworthy of attention. But the Spirit who inspired Scripture saw fit to record them, and they carry a real lesson: the worship of God is to be conducted in order, continually, every servant knowing his charge and his season. The courses endured to the New Testament, when Zacharias ministered in the order of his course (Luke 1:8) and met the angel at the appointed hour of incense.

The principle to recover is that the God of order ordains both the substance and the arrangement of His worship. David set the courses by lot, yet the ordering was as the LORD God of Israel had commanded (1 Chr 24:19); even the lot was disposed by the LORD. The pattern teaches that ministry is to be carried on decently and in order, for God is not the author of confusion but of peace (1 Cor 14:40), and that faithful service in one’s appointed place—however ordinary the week, however unremarkable the turn—is the will of God for His servants. The unglamorous course of Abia was the very place where heaven broke in.

etymology: From Levitical + musician; the Levites appointed by David to lead the song and music of the LORD’s house.
biblical_def: The Levitical musicians were the Levites whom David appointed to the service of song in the house of the LORD, to prophesy with harps, with psalteries, and with cymbals, and to give thanks and praise unto the LORD. He set apart the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, skilful men, two hundred fourscore and eight in number, to minister before the ark with continual praise, that the voice of thanksgiving might be heard in the sanctuary. Their ministry was no mere performance but a sacred office, ordained alongside the sacrifices, for when the burnt offering began, the song of the LORD began also with the trumpets. At the dedication of Solomon’s temple, when the singers and trumpeters were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD, the glory of the LORD filled the house. The Levitical musicians teach that the praise of God is His own appointment, to be offered skilfully, reverently, and according to His command, joined to the worship of His altar. They foreshadow the praise of the whole church, the spiritual sacrifice of the fruit of our lips, and the song of the redeemed about the throne. The dictionary honors the Levitical musicians as the divinely-ordained leaders of sacred praise, a witness that song is a holy ministry in the worship of God, to be rendered with skill and reverence to His glory, and that the praise of His people is dear to Him and crowned with His presence.
webster_summary: The Levites David appointed to lead the song of the LORD’s house with skill and reverence; a witness that sacred praise is a holy, divinely-ordained ministry.

By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name.
corruption_summary: Sacred song is reduced to performance and entertainment, or its skill despised; Scripture sets praise as a holy, ordained ministry rendered reverently to God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two opposite errors attend sacred song. The first turns the music of worship into performance and entertainment, where the skill of the musicians draws the eye to themselves and the congregation becomes an audience—the very opposite of the Levitical office, which was to lead the people in giving thanks unto the LORD. The second despises skill and care in praise, as though reverence forbade excellence; but David appointed skilful men (1 Chr 25:1), and the praise of God deserves the best we can offer.

The principle to recover is that sacred praise is a holy ministry, ordained by God, joined to His worship, and offered to His glory. The Levitical musicians were set apart by David alongside the sacrifices (1 Chr 23:5); their song began with the burnt offering, and when the singers and trumpeters were as one in praising the LORD, the house was filled with His glory (2 Chr 5:13). Their ministry foreshadows the praise of the whole church, the sacrifice of praise, the fruit of our lips (Heb 13:15). Worship-song is therefore neither a concert nor a careless thing, but a reverent, skilful, congregational ministry, rendered to God and crowned with His presence.

etymology: From Levitical + cities; the forty-eight cities given to the Levites throughout Israel, having no tribal land of their own.
biblical_def: The Levitical cities were the forty-eight cities, with their suburbs for cattle, which the LORD commanded Israel to give to the tribe of Levi out of the inheritances of the other tribes, since Levi received no territorial portion of its own. For the LORD was the inheritance of Levi: the priesthood of the LORD is their inheritance, and the offerings of the people their portion. So the Levites were scattered throughout all Israel, dwelling among every tribe, that they might teach Jacob the LORD’s judgments and Israel His law, and minister in the worship of God. Among the forty-eight, six were the cities of refuge, to which the manslayer might flee. The scattering of Levi fulfilled the old word over Jacob’s sons, that Levi should be divided and scattered in Israel—a curse pronounced over Levi’s violence turned, by grace and zeal for the LORD, into a blessing, for their dispersion became the means of teaching the whole land. The dictionary honors the Levitical cities as a testimony that those who serve at the altar are to live of the altar, that the teaching of God’s law was to be spread through every part of His people, and that a curse may be transformed by grace into a ministry—Levi scattered, not for ruin, but that the knowledge of the LORD might fill the land.
webster_summary: The forty-eight cities given to Levi, who had no tribal land, scattered through Israel to teach the law; a curse turned by grace into a ministry of the LORD’s knowledge.

corruption_summary: The Levitical cities are read as mere administrative geography; Scripture frames them as the LORD being Levi’s inheritance and a curse turned to teaching ministry.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the merely administrative reading that treats the Levitical cities as a land-allotment scheme, dry geography of no spiritual weight. But Scripture frames them with rich meaning. Levi received no inheritance of land, for the LORD God of Israel was their inheritance (Jos 13:33): those who serve at His altar are to live of the altar, content with the LORD as their portion.

The principle to recover is that the scattering of Levi was a curse transformed by grace into a ministry. Jacob had pronounced over Levi’s fierce anger, I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel (Gen 49:7)—a word of judgment on Levi’s violence. Yet at Sinai Levi’s zeal for the LORD turned the curse, so that the same scattering became the means of blessing: the Levites, dwelling in their forty-eight cities throughout the land (Num 35:7), were placed to teach Jacob the LORD’s judgments and Israel His law (Deu 33:10). What was pronounced for ruin God made a ministry, that the knowledge of the LORD might fill the whole land—a pattern of how grace turns even our judgments into instruments of good.

etymology: From Exodus 28:36; the inscription engraved on the golden plate of the high priest’s mitre.
biblical_def: Holiness to the LORD was the inscription engraved, like the engravings of a signet, upon the plate of pure gold worn on the forefront of the high priest’s mitre. It declared the whole purpose and character of the priesthood and the sanctuary: that all was set apart, consecrated, devoted wholly to the LORD. The plate was upon Aaron’s forehead always, that he might bear the iniquity of the holy things, and that the gifts of the people might be accepted before the LORD—for even Israel’s holy offerings needed a holiness not their own to make them acceptable. The phrase reaches beyond the mitre: Zechariah prophesied a day when Holiness to the LORD should be engraved even upon the bells of the horses, and every pot in Jerusalem and Judah should be holiness unto the LORD—the whole of life, common and sacred alike, consecrated to God. So the inscription is at once a present truth and a promise: the people of God are a holy nation, a royal priesthood, called to be holy as He is holy, and the day comes when all things shall be made holiness to the LORD. It is fulfilled supremely in Christ, the true High Priest, who is Himself the Holy One, and who sanctifies His people that they may be unto Him a peculiar treasure. The dictionary honors Holiness to the LORD as the motto of the consecrated life, the inscription that should be written over the believer’s whole walk, that whatever he does, in word or deed, he do all to the glory of God.
webster_summary: The inscription on the high priest’s golden plate, declaring all set apart to the LORD; a motto of the consecrated life, fulfilled in Christ and to fill all things.
webster_full: HOLINESS TO THE LORD, the inscription on the high priest’s golden plate.

corruption_summary: Holiness is reduced to mere ritual purity or sentimental piety; Scripture sets it as entire consecration to the LORD, of life and worship, fulfilled in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the shrinking of holiness into either mere ritual purity—a matter of ceremonies and externals—or sentimental piety, a warm religious feeling. But the inscription Holiness to the LORD declares something far weightier: entire consecration, the whole being set apart and devoted to God. Even Israel’s holy gifts needed the high priest, bearing this plate, to make them accepted (Exo 28:38), for nothing of ours is holy enough in itself to stand before Him.

The principle to recover is the call to entire consecration of life and worship, fulfilled in Christ. The motto was not confined to the mitre; Zechariah foresaw the day when Holiness to the LORD should be written even on the bells of the horses, and every common pot be holy (Zec 14:20)—the whole of life, common and sacred, consecrated to God. This is the believer’s calling: Be ye holy; for I am holy (1 Pet 1:16). It is grounded not in our own purity but in Christ, the true High Priest who is Himself the Holy One and who sanctifies His people. Holiness to the LORD is therefore the motto that should be written over the believer’s whole walk, that whatever he does he do all to the glory of God.
roots_summary: From Exodus 28:36; the inscription on the high priest’s golden plate, declaring all consecrated to the LORD, the motto of the holy life fulfilled in Christ.

etymology: From without the camp (Heb 13:13); the place of reproach and of the sin offering, where Christ suffered.
biblical_def: Outside the camp—in the Authorized Version, without the camp—is the place of reproach, of uncleanness, and of the sin offering under the law, taken up by the writer to the Hebrews as the place where Christ suffered and where His people are called to follow Him. Under the law, the bodies of the beasts whose blood was brought into the sanctuary for sin were burned without the camp; there too the leper dwelt, and the unclean, and there the condemned were taken to die. So the Hebrews writer reasons: Jesus also, that He might sanctify the people with His own blood, suffered without the gate. He was led outside the city, to the place of the skull, bearing the reproach of the condemned, that His blood might cleanse His people. And the exhortation follows: Let us go forth therefore unto Him without the camp, bearing His reproach—for here we have no continuing city, but seek one to come. To go outside the camp is to leave behind the security, the approval, and the religious establishment of this world, to share the reproach of the crucified Christ, and to count His shame greater riches than the world’s honour. The dictionary honors this phrase as the call to identify with the rejected Christ, to bear the reproach the world heaps on His name, and to seek the city that hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
webster_summary: The place of reproach and the sin offering, where Christ suffered without the gate; the call to leave the world’s approval and bear His reproach, seeking the city to come.

To leave the world’s approval and seek the city to come.
scriptures: For the bodies of those beasts, whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest for sin, are burned without the camp.
Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate.

corruption_summary: The call outside the camp is softened by a religion that craves the world’s approval; Scripture summons the believer to share the rejected Christ’s reproach.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the instinct, ever present in the church, to soften or evade the call outside the camp—to seek instead the approval, the security, and the honour of the world, to keep a place within its establishment, and to shrink from the reproach of the crucified Christ. A religion that craves the world’s acceptance cannot follow a Lord who was led without the gate to die.

The principle to recover is identification with the rejected Christ. The pattern is set in the law: the bodies of the sin offerings were burned without the camp (Heb 13:11), in the place of uncleanness and reproach; and there Jesus suffered, that He might sanctify His people with His own blood (Heb 13:12). The exhortation follows inescapably: Let us go forth therefore unto Him without the camp, bearing His reproach (Heb 13:13). To follow Christ is to leave the camp of the world’s approval, to count His shame greater riches than its honour, and to seek not a continuing city here but the one to come (Heb 13:14). The reproach of Christ, borne gladly, is the mark of His true people.

etymology: From sacred + lot; the casting of lots to discern the will of God, as with the Urim and Thummim.
biblical_def: The sacred lot was the appointed means by which, under the old covenant, the will of God was sought and discerned in matters left to His direct disposing—the casting of lots, and especially the Urim and Thummim borne in the breastplate of the high priest. By lot the land of Canaan was divided among the tribes; by lot the courses of the priests were ordered; by lot Achan was discovered, and Jonah’s ship found out the guilty; by Urim the LORD answered, or refused to answer, the inquiries of His people. The principle is given in the proverb: The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD—for the lot was not chance but the ordering of God, who governs even the fall of the dice. In the New Testament the apostles cast lots to choose Matthias, the last recorded use, before the Spirit was given at Pentecost; thereafter the church is guided by the completed Scripture and the indwelling Spirit, and the sacred lot ceases. The dictionary honors the sacred lot as a witness that nothing is left to chance, that the LORD disposes all things, even those men call random; and it marks the change of administration, that the people of God now seek His will not by lot or Urim but by His sufficient word and the leading of His Spirit, the closed canon having replaced the casting of lots.
webster_summary: The casting of lots and the Urim to discern God’s will under the old covenant; a witness that nothing is chance, the lot’s disposing being wholly of the LORD.

corruption_summary: The lot is misread as endorsing chance and divination, or revived as a present method of guidance; Scripture shows God’s sovereign disposing and the lot’s ceasing.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors attend the sacred lot. The first reads it as an endorsement of chance or divination, as though Scripture sanctioned fortune-telling and games of luck. But the lot was never chance: the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD (Pro 16:33), and the sacred lot, with the Urim, was a means God Himself appointed for His people to seek His will (Exo 28:30). The second error would revive the casting of lots as a present method of divine guidance, ignoring the change of administration.

The principle to recover is twofold: the sovereignty of God over all that men call random, and the cessation of the lot under the new covenant. Nothing is chance; the LORD disposes the fall of the lot, the roll of the dice, the seeming accident—a great comfort to His people, who know their times are in His hand. Yet the sacred lot itself has ceased. Its last recorded use chose Matthias before Pentecost (Acts 1:26); thereafter the church, having the completed Scripture and the indwelling Spirit, seeks God’s will not by Urim or lot but by His sufficient word. The closed canon has replaced the casting of lots, and the believer is guided by the Scriptures, prayer, and sanctified wisdom, not by chance.

etymology: From Leviticus 2:13; the salt commanded with every offering, a token of the perpetual covenant.
biblical_def: The salt of the covenant is the salt which the LORD commanded to be offered with every sacrifice: with all thine offerings thou shalt offer salt; neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the covenant of thy God to be lacking from thy meat offering. Salt, which preserves from corruption and does not itself decay, was the fitting token of the covenant’s perpetuity and incorruptibility. So the LORD speaks of His covenant with the priesthood as a covenant of salt for ever, and of the kingdom given to David as a covenant of salt—an everlasting, unbreakable bond. To eat salt with another was, in the East, to enter a sacred bond of fellowship and fidelity. The salt upon the offerings declared that the worshipper drew near in covenant, and that the covenant of God endures and preserves. The figure is taken up by the Lord, who calls His disciples the salt of the earth, and bids them have salt in themselves, and be at peace one with another. The dictionary honors the salt of the covenant as a token of the perpetuity and incorruptibility of God’s covenant with His people, a witness that the bond He makes does not decay, and a call to the covenant fidelity, purity, and preserving witness that the salt signifies—that the people of His covenant are to be themselves a savour of incorruption in a perishing world.
webster_summary: The salt commanded with every offering, a token of the perpetual, incorruptible covenant; God’s bond that does not decay, and a call to covenant fidelity and witness.

corruption_summary: The salt is dismissed as quaint ritual detail; Scripture makes it a token of the covenant’s perpetuity and a call to incorruptible covenant fidelity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the dismissal of the salt as quaint ritual detail—a culinary footnote in the sacrificial law, easily passed over. But the LORD invested it with covenant meaning: it is the salt of the covenant of thy God (Lev 2:13), and He speaks of His abiding bonds as covenants of salt for ever (Num 18:19; 2 Chr 13:5). Salt preserves from corruption and does not itself decay; it is therefore the fit token of a covenant that endures and cannot be broken.

The principle to recover is the perpetuity and incorruptibility of God’s covenant, and the covenant fidelity it summons in His people. The bond God makes does not decay; His covenant of salt stands for ever, a comfort to all who rest in His unbreakable promise. And the figure passes to the disciple: Christ calls His people the salt of the earth, and bids them have salt in themselves, and have peace one with another (Mark 9:50). The people of the covenant are to be themselves a savour of incorruption—faithful, pure, preserving—in a perishing world, lest the salt lose its saltness and be good for nothing. The salt of the covenant is thus both promise and charge: God’s bond endures; let His people be true to it.
